rows: Suspected scabies cases in communal settings should receive clinical assessment.
Diagnosed cases should be treated promptly.
Close contacts should be identified over the relevant exposure period.
Coordinated treatment of cases and contacts helps break transmission.
Two or more epidemiologically linked cases within the defined period can constitute an outbreak.
Crusted scabies requires enhanced contact assessment because it is more infectious.
Settings should coordinate cleaning, communication and transfer precautions.
Complex or recurrent outbreaks may require health-protection-team support.
An itchy rash or shared residence does not establish scabies or an outbreak.
Conclusions require diagnosis, contact history, timing, clinical type, coordinated treatment and epidemiological linkage.
Suspected polio and acute flaccid paralysis require prompt surveillance action.
Public-health and laboratory teams use national guidelines for investigation.
Appropriate clinical and stool samples are required for confirmation.
Enhanced enterovirus surveillance supports polio detection.
Case management includes exposure and vaccination assessment.
Contacts may require public-health assessment and post-exposure measures.
Laboratories handling poliovirus must follow containment requirements.
Investigation contributes to the global polio-eradication commitment.
Acute weakness or an enterovirus result does not establish paralytic polio.
Conclusions require clinical pattern, vaccination, travel, specimens, virology, exposure and public-health evidence.
Anthrax is a rare infection caused by the spore-forming bacterium Bacillus anthracis.
Suspected cases require prompt clinical and public-health assessment.
Clinical presentation depends on the route of exposure.
Laboratory testing should follow specialist reference arrangements.
Treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis depend on risk and clinical circumstances.
Vaccination can be relevant for specified occupational or exposure groups.
Environmental samples require controlled collection and interpretation.
Imported animal products and contaminated materials can be relevant exposure sources.
A suspicious powder, animal product or skin lesion does not establish anthrax.
Conclusions require exposure route, clinical features, specimen, laboratory, environmental and public-health evidence.
Cryptosporidium can spread through contaminated water, food, animals or direct faecal contact.
Watery diarrhoea is a common symptom.
Laboratory testing is needed to confirm cryptosporidiosis.
Handwashing with soap and water is an important preventive measure.
People should avoid swallowing recreational water.
Symptomatic people should follow exclusion advice for work, school and food handling.
Swimming should be avoided for the recommended period after diarrhoea stops.
UKHSA supports source investigation and outbreak control.
Farm contact or diarrhoea does not establish cryptosporidiosis.
Conclusions require symptoms, laboratory, water or animal exposure, timing, setting and outbreak evidence.
